Metadata.title: AgiMate — a multiagent harness
Metadata.description: Not one assistant but a system of agents: each with its own model, its own instructions, its own access and its own skills. Shared between them: the rules, a log of every call, and a board to work on together. Keys and passwords stay in the platform and never reach the model.
Metadata.ogDescription: The harness around any language model: tools, keys to your systems, rules checked before the call, and a log of every action. As many agents as you need, each with its own settings.

hero.title: A multiagent
hero.subtitle: Not an assistant — a system of agents. The harness around any language model gives them tools, keys to your systems, rules and a log. As many agents as you need, each one its own: its own model, its own instructions, its own access, its own skills — and none of them ever sees a key.

steps.label: The harness
steps.sub: agents with their own models, rights and skills

steps.label: Action
steps.sub: in your system, not advice in a chat

harness.title: What a harness is
harness.subtitle: A language model does one thing — write text. Everything that turns text into work sits around it. One harness for the whole system; the settings belong to each agent.

items.title: Hands — the tools
items.tech: The concrete calls that connections bring in: MCP servers, your own API behind a key, connectors to Telegram, your phone and your computer. A tool appears for an agent together with the binding.
items.plain: What the agent can do at all: send a message, file a task, read a spreadsheet. The toolbox.

items.title: Craft — the skills
items.tech: A skill is written know-how for using tools: the order of steps, the rules, and the connectors it needs. It is versioned, reused across agents, and picked from a shared catalogue.
items.plain: Tools are what an agent can do. A skill is how well it handles them: which one to reach for, in what order, when to stop and ask. Without it the agent holds the hammer without knowing what for.

items.title: Keys — held by the harness, not the agent
items.tech: A connection's credentials stay on the platform side. The agent only ever gets tool descriptions and calls them by name — no key, no token, no password reaches the model.
items.plain: The agent doesn't know your passwords. It never sees them: it says "send the email", and the harness supplies the key, outside the model.

items.title: Rails — rules checked before the call
items.tech: Allow or deny an individual tool and its parameters, up to closing a connection entirely.
items.plain: "Reading is fine, deleting isn't." Checked before the agent touches the service, not after.

items.title: Trail — the log of every action
items.tech: The run, its steps, every call with parameters and result, token spend per model.
items.plain: You can see what the agent actually did and why. Not "it seems to have broken something", but a line with the parameters and the answer.

items.title: Team — agents in one harness
items.tech: An agentic team over a shared task board, updating live in the dashboard.
items.plain: One agent isn't enough for the job — put a second one beside it. You can see who took what and where it stands.

harness.callout: An agent can be talked into things — it is a language model, after all. But it cannot hand over a key: it doesn't have one. The most it can do is try to call a tool, and that runs into the rules and stays in the log.

agents.title: Every agent its own
agents.subtitle: One agent holding every key and every tool is exactly the all-or-nothing problem. A system of narrow agents is safer, more accurate and cheaper.

axes.title: Its own model
axes.tech: The provider and the priority list of models are set on the agent, separately for chat, vision and image generation.
axes.plain: An expensive model where thinking is needed, a cheap one where it's shuffling data. You pay per job, not one flat rate for everything.

axes.title: Its own instructions
axes.tech: Each agent carries its own instruction text — from a ready-made role or from scratch.
axes.plain: Each has its own manner and its own ground rules. One answers a customer briefly and politely, another works through the numbers in detail.

axes.title: Its own access
axes.tech: Connections are bound to a specific agent, and inside a binding there are rules for individual tools and their parameters.
axes.plain: Like clearances for staff. One holds the keys to email, another to the spreadsheets, and nobody holds keys to everything.

axes.title: Its own skills
axes.tech: The skill set is assembled on the agent; another agent's tools never show up in it.
axes.plain: An agent can do exactly what its role needs. Less lying around means less chance of reaching for the wrong tool.

items.title: All or nothing
items.description: The assistant gets access to everything at once — email, files, calendar. One bad tool and the boundaries are gone.

items.title: Black box
items.description: You don't know what the assistant did: which tool it called, with what parameters, what came back. Nothing to investigate with.

items.title: Someone else's model, someone else's bill
items.description: The model was chosen for you, spend is invisible, tokens are resold at a markup. Switching providers isn't an option.

howItWorks.title: How it works
howItWorks.subtitle: Everything rests on triggers: an event arrives, the system wakes the agents it belongs to, hands them the skills for it and checks the rights on every call.
howItWorks.parallelNote: In parallel, not one after another
howItWorks.channelsLabel: The answer goes to your channel
howItWorks.boardNote: The board is yours to watch, and it updates live

tabs.label: Triggers
tabs.title: It all starts with an event
tabs.description: A trigger is what agents react to: you wrote to an agent or sent a file, someone left a review of your product, new mail arrived, another agent asked for data, a scheduled time came round. Which triggers reach which agent is yours to decide.
sources: A message or file from you

tabs.label: Launch
tabs.title: The system wakes the agents and hands out skills
tabs.description: The agents the trigger belongs to stand up. Each is handed the skills this particular event needs — not their whole set. They start together and work in parallel, without waiting for one another.

tabs.label: Work
tabs.title: A tool only fires once the rights check passes
tabs.description: An agent picks from the tools available to it, and every call goes through a check: a denied tool never fires, and the attempt stays in the log. The answer can go back through any channel you talk to it on.

tabs.label: Team and board
tabs.title: Agents work it out on the board
tabs.description: When agents work as a team they ask each other clarifying questions and keep a shared task board: statuses, assignees, comments. The board is open to you too — you can see who took what, what they decided on, and what the context was.
tabs.question: What's the budget?

useCases.title: What you can build today
useCases.subtitle: Scenarios made of parts that already exist in the dashboard — each one shows what it's assembled from

items.title: An agent in Telegram
items.description: Set up a channel: the Telegram connector, an incoming-message trigger, a reply tool. The agent answers per your instructions and the conversation is stored as sessions you can read in the dashboard.

items.title: A scheduled check
items.description: A connector job runs on a schedule: the agent visits an external service, checks what matters and writes to you. Jobs can be paused or run right now.

items.title: Reacting to an event
items.description: An external system sends a webhook — the agent parses the event and takes the next step. Every delivery and every tool call stays in the trigger logs.

items.title: An agent on your device
items.description: The Android and desktop apps are connectors to your own hardware, and there is nowhere else to get them. Notifications, calls and device events become triggers, and the agent answers with a push, spoken text or a command carried out on the device.

items.title: An agent in your IDE
items.description: Over the ACP protocol the agent plugs into your editor and works next to the code — with the same skills, access rules and log as everywhere else.

items.title: Your own service as a tool
items.description: Connect your API as a key-authenticated app or an MCP server — its methods become the agent's tools. What exactly it may do is up to your rules.

items.title: A team of agents on a shared board
items.description: One agent is not the ceiling: assemble a team and give it a shared board. Tasks with statuses, an assigned agent, comments in the thread. Changes reach the dashboard in real time.

items.title: The agent only sees what's bound
items.description: Until a connection is bound to an agent, its tools don't exist for that agent. Bindings are visible from both sides: on the agent and on the connection.

items.title: Rules are checked before the call
items.description: Allow or deny a specific tool, constrain its parameters, close a connection entirely. The rule fires before the external service is ever contacted, and the denial goes to the log.

items.title: Every action logged
items.description: Who called what, when, with what result. Errors and policy denials are collected separately, so you know where to look.

models.title: Your model, your key

sections.title: What the service is
sections.body: AgiMate is a platform for building AI agents: you assemble an agent from skills, grant it access to tools, and talk to it through channels.

sections.title: Early access
sections.body: The service runs in early access. Expect occasional downtime, changes in functionality, and limits on usage volume.

sections.title: Your content and keys
sections.body: Agent instructions, conversations, and third-party provider keys belong to you. We use them only to make the service work.

sections.title: Responsibility
sections.body: The agent acts on your instructions, within the boundaries you set. Review your access rules before granting an agent access to sensitive tools.

sections.title: Changes

meta.title: Privacy Policy — AgiMate
meta.description: What data AgiMate stores, where keys and logs live. The document is in progress — the substance is set out here.

Privacy.title: Privacy Policy
Privacy.draftNotice: The final wording will land before public launch. While the document is being prepared, here is how things work today.

sections.title: What we store
sections.body: Your OAuth provider profile (name and email address), the agents you create, skills, connections, and your conversations with agents.

sections.title: Tokens and keys
sections.body: The refresh token lives in an HTTP-only cookie and is unreachable from JavaScript. LLM provider keys and connection secrets are stored server-side and are never shown again in the interface.

sections.title: Third-party services
sections.body: Model requests go to the provider whose key you connected. Tool calls go to the services you connected yourself.

sections.title: Logs
sections.body: We keep a log of tool calls and triggers — it exists for your own troubleshooting and is visible in the dashboard.

sections.title: Self-hosted
sections.body: When deployed on your own server, data never leaves your infrastructure.

sections.title: Deletion
sections.body: Write to us and we'll delete your account and the data attached to it.

Privacy.contactBody: Write to us in the community chat — we'll answer.
